sections.title: Reading Passage 1 - Urban beekeeping
sections.instructions: Questions 1-5: choose True, False or Not Given. Questions 6-9: complete the sentences with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. Questions 10-13: answer with NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER.
sections.passage:
A. In the past twenty years, beekeeping has moved from the countryside into the centre of major cities. Rooftops, school playgrounds and railway embankments now host hives in London, Berlin and Toronto. Supporters argue that urban hives raise public awareness of pollinating insects. Critics answer that the honeybee is a managed livestock species rather than an endangered wild pollinator, so the practice has little to do with conservation.

B. Ecologists at the University of Sussex carried out a three-year survey of flowering plants in Brighton and Hove. They recorded insects visiting 240 plant species. Wild bees, hoverflies and butterflies accounted for 60 per cent of the visits, and managed honeybees for the remainder. In districts where hive numbers were highest, wild bee diversity fell by almost a third.

C. The explanation appears to be competition. A single hive may contain 50,000 bees, each foraging within a radius of roughly three kilometres. Where hives are clustered, managed colonies can drain the nectar and pollen that solitary bees and bumblebees depend on. The effect is strongest in late summer, when wildflowers are scarce.

D. Some city authorities have responded by limiting hive numbers. Paris now requires a permit for new hives on public buildings, and Amsterdam has stopped issuing licences in districts where wild bee populations are already under stress. Other councils have taken a different route, replacing mown grass with wildflower meadows. The meadow programme in Brighton increased the abundance of wild flowers fourfold in five years, and the local bumblebee population grew with it.

E. Researchers agree on one point. Whether or not urban hives are useful, planting is not optional. Flowers help every pollinator, whereas hives help one species that is already abundant. For a city that wants to support insects, a verge of unmown wildflowers may achieve more than a rooftop of hives.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2 - The cost of the open-plan office
sections.instructions: Questions 14-17: choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Questions 18-21: match each statement with the correct paragraph, A-E. Questions 22-26: complete the summary with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.
sections.passage:
A. Open-plan offices were designed to encourage collaboration. Yet surveys consistently report that employees in open-plan settings are more distracted, not less. A study of 42,000 workers in the United States and Europe found that open-plan employees reported 70 per cent more interruptions and, paradoxically, fewer face-to-face conversations than colleagues in enclosed rooms.

B. Part of the problem is speech. Human attention is drawn to intelligible speech more strongly than to almost any other sound, because a nearby conversation competes directly with the language we are already processing. Constant, meaningless noise such as the hum of air conditioning is far less disruptive, even when it is louder.

C. This finding has practical consequences. Sound masking systems broadcast a soft, unobtrusive sound through ceiling speakers. They raise the background level so that speech becomes less intelligible without becoming louder to the listener. In trials in nine offices, masking reduced self-reported distractions by 19 per cent and improved performance on a proofreading task by roughly 8 per cent.

D. Other designers favour small enclosed booths for telephone calls. Booths are effective but expensive, and staff must be persuaded to move to them. A cheaper measure is to rearrange desks so that colleagues who talk on the phone are not seated facing one another, which reduces visual and acoustic interference without any construction work.

E. None of these measures removes the underlying conflict. Organisations claim to want both communication and concentration, and the two requirements pull in opposite directions. The most successful workplaces decide, department by department, which of the two matters more, and design accordingly.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 - Repair, do not replace
sections.instructions: Questions 27-30: choose Yes, No or Not Given. Questions 31-34: complete the notes with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER. Questions 35-36: choose TWO letters. Questions 37-40: label the plan, using NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS.
sections.passage:
A. The first repair cafe opened in Amsterdam in 2009. Volunteers with tools and spare time offered to mend broken household items free of charge: toasters, lamps, bicycles, clothes and occasionally computers. The idea spread quickly through Europe. By 2024 more than 3,000 repair cafes were registered worldwide, with the largest numbers in Germany and the Netherlands.

B. The movement's founders describe two aims. The first is practical: keeping usable objects out of landfill. The second is educational. Visitors are encouraged to watch the repair, and about half of all sessions end with the owner having learned enough to attempt a similar repair alone.

C. Measuring the environmental benefit is harder than it appears. One widely quoted estimate claims that repair cafes save thousands of tonnes of material each year. A 2023 analysis, however, found that the figure was produced by multiplying the number of cafes by an assumed weight per repaired item, an assumption that had never been tested. The researchers placed the reliable figure at less than a fifth of the published estimate.

D. Manufacturers are an awkward partner. Some provide spare parts; others design products that cannot be opened without special tools, a practice campaigners call economic obsolescence. European legislation adopted in 2021 requires spare parts for certain appliances for up to ten years, but repairers report that parts are often unavailable in practice.

E. The social effect may be the most durable. A repair cafe is rarely quiet. Volunteers describe the event as a meeting place where people who would not otherwise meet exchange skills, and where older participants are treated as experts rather than as people needing help. Registration figures measure machines repaired, but the cafes themselves measure conversations.
